title: Why You Should Never Use Restrictive Methods With Difficult Students ods-with-difficult-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin critiques the common tendency to corral and restrict difficult students—keeping them apart from certain peers or situations to preempt trouble. He argues this approach fails because it labels students and reinforces the identity of being a 'behavior problem,' while also being unsustainable and exhausting for teachers. Instead, he advocates giving difficult students the same freedom-within-boundaries afforded to everyone else, holding them accountable through the same predetermined, universally applied classroom management plan. He frames this consistency, paired with vigilant observation, as the only strategy that genuinely changes behavior over time.
points: Restricting where difficult students can go or who they can be near is a commonly used but ultimately ineffective avoidance strategy.
Singling students out with individualized restrictions reinforces their identity as a 'behavior problem' rather than a regular student.
Difficult students need the same classroom management plan and freedom-within-boundaries given to every other student, not special restrictions.
Freedom paired with consistent, universal accountability lets students experience consequences without carrying a permanent label.
The strategy only works with consistency, a protected relationship, and vigilant observation, since freedom requires verification.
quotes: The tendency is to corral difficult students, to limit what they can do, where they can go, and who they can be with.
It whispers in their ear again and again that they are their misbehavior.
The truth is that difficult students need to feel like regular students before they can start behaving like regular students.
It only works if you’re consistent. It only works if you nurture and protect the relationship between you.
It is, in fact, the only surefire way to change behavior, to send them on their way after their time with you resurrected, transformed, and ready to take on the world.
